Replace each `___` with code, remove `#| eval: false` and run the chunk. Write your prediction before you run each join, then write the result.

The tables come with the dplyr package.

```{r}
#| label: setup
pacman::p_load(tidyverse)
```

## Look at the tables

```{r}
#| label: look-members
band_members
```

```{r}
#| label: look-instruments
band_instruments
```

Which column do both tables share?

Answer: `name`.

Who appears in both tables?

Answer: John and Paul. Mick is only in `band_members`, and Keith is only in `band_instruments`.

## Your turn 1: left_join()

Complete the key.

```{r}
#| label: turn-1
band_members |>
  left_join(band_instruments, join_by(name))
```

Prediction: 3 rows. Result: 3 rows.

Who has `NA` in `plays`? Mick. He is in `band_members` but not in `band_instruments`, so there is no instrument to fill in.

## Your turn 2: swap the tables

```{r}
#| label: turn-2
#| eval: false
band_instruments |>
  left_join(band_members, join_by(name))
```

## Your turn 3: inner_join()

Keep only the people who have a band and an instrument. Complete the function name.

```{r}
#| label: turn-3
band_members |>
  inner_join(band_instruments, join_by(name))
```

Prediction: 2 rows. Result: 2 rows.

Who is missing from the result, and why? Mick and Keith. `inner_join()` keeps only the names that are in both tables. Mick has no instrument and Keith has no band.

## Your turn 4: full_join()

Keep all four people. Complete the function name.

```{r}
#| label: turn-4
band_members |>
  full_join(band_instruments, join_by(name))
```

Prediction: 4 rows. Result: 4 rows.

Where do you see `NA`? Mick has `NA` in `plays` (no instrument), and Keith has `NA` in `band` (no band).

## Your turn 5: anti_join()

Who is in `band_members` and has no instrument?

```{r}
#| label: turn-5
band_members |>
  anti_join(band_instruments, join_by(name))
```

Prediction: Mick. Result: Mick (1 row). He is the only member with no match in `band_instruments`.
